summary: Three distribution lists for sending out Network documents such as RFCs. One is for sites sending their own documents to liaisons, and the others are for the Network Information Center to reach other participants and station agents. These were postal lists with names and addresses, not email lists. It was replaced by RFC 300.

eli5.summary: This is an address book of who should get a paper copy of each new note, and which list each kind of sender should use. It is mail by post, not email.

subtitle: Three distribution lists for sending RFCs and documents across the ARPANET

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET grew, there was a need for multiple distribution lists to send RFCs and documents to different groups of participants and their local representatives.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 211 defines three lists: List A for site liaisons to receive RFCs first, List B for other network participants, and List C for NIC Station Agents who handle local distribution.
tldr.outcome: This organized approach to document distribution remained the standard model through several RFC revisions. It was replaced by RFC 300.

facts.label: NIC update frequency
facts.value: Once a week or as needed

today: RFC 211 is historic and obsoleted. It was replaced by RFC 300, which updated the mailing lists as the network continued to grow. This RFC is significant for establishing the three-tier distribution model for network documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 211 defines how network documents should be distributed in August 1971. The RFC specifies three separate mailing lists to serve different purposes as the ARPANET expanded beyond its original sites.

The RFC notes that sites sending their own documents should use List A to reach liaisons quickly, while the Network Information Center (NIC) uses Lists B and C for broader distribution to non-site participants and to station agents.
sections.eli5: When someone sends a new network paper, different groups of people need to get it. This explains which list to use.

sections.title: The Three Distribution Lists
sections.content:
List A (Initial Distribution) includes all network liaisons and others who should receive initial distribution of RFCs from either NIC or from sites. These recipients also get selected catalogs and formal documents from NIC.

List B (NIC Distribution) consists of network participants who will receive all formal documents sent from NIC, either when mailed to liaisons or when sent to station agents.

List C (Station Agents) lists the local representatives at each site. Station agents receive copies of all documents sent to liaisons, plus additional materials. NIC sends mailings to station agents once a week or more frequently as needed.
sections.eli5: List A: The main people who need papers. List B: Other people on the network. List C: Local helpers who pass papers around at each site.

sections.title: Scope and Geographic Coverage
sections.content:
The RFC covers about 25 major sites and institutions, expanding beyond RFC 155. It includes universities, research companies, and new international locations. The text recommends air mail for all but local deliveries.

This list supersedes RFC 168 and represents the ARPANET structure as it existed in August 1971. Like RFC 155, it reflects a time when physical mail was the only way to distribute documents across the network.
sections.eli5: This is a bigger list than the last one, with new places added. It still uses postal mail, but with air mail for far-away places.
